examEntry.label: Pearson Edexcel IGCSE 4AA1
examEntry.papers: Paper 1 Reading, Summary and Grammar (4AA1/01): 2 hours 15 minutes, 75 marks, 60% (reading on two texts 49 marks, summary of a third text 6, grammar 20). Paper 2 Writing (4AA1/02): 1 hour 30 minutes, 50 marks, 40%, two 25-mark tasks from a choice of three.
examEntry.privateCandidates: Written papers only: no listening paper and no speaking test, so nothing has to be conducted by a teacher at the centre (unlike 1AA0 Paper 2).
examEntry.choice: Group A (default): 4AA1, written papers only, January and June series. Group B: GCSE 1AA0 (four skills, Foundation or Higher), which suits pupils whose Arabic is not at first-language level and needs a centre that conducts the speaking test; entry is decided per pupil by July of Year 10.
notes: 4AA1 is a first-language qualification. We found no Pearson International GCSE in Arabic as a foreign language, so 4AA1 is the matching International GCSE.

It asks more than 1AA0 in reading and grammar: longer authentic texts, a summary task, and grammar questions that use grammatical terminology. Add explicit grammar teaching (with the Arabic terms), summary writing and extended writing to the 1AA0 course from Year 10.
1AA0 listening, speaking and translation are not examined in 4AA1. Keep them in lessons for language development, but weight Year 11 towards reading, grammar and writing.
The 4AA1 topics (youth, education, media, culture, sport and leisure, travel and tourism, work, environment, health, technology) overlap with the 1AA0 themes.
Both groups follow the same Year 10 to 11 theme order from the school's GCSE scheme of work; 4AA1 entrants add summary and grammar work, 1AA0 entrants add listening and speaking practice.
1AA0 summer 2027 (Pearson final timetable): Paper 2 speaking in the centre's April to May window; Papers 1 and 3 Mon 24 May (afternoon); Paper 4 Mon 7 Jun (afternoon).
TO CONFIRM: which TGA pupils are entered for 1AA0 and at which tier, and the centre for each 1AA0 speaking test.

assessment.duration: Foundation 35 min; Higher 45 min (each includes 5 min reading time)
assessment.content: All five themes.
assessment.format: Multiple-response and short open-response. Foundation: Section A 12 questions in English, Section B two in Arabic. Higher: Section A two in Arabic, Section B eight in English. No dictionaries.

assessment.title: Speaking in Arabic
assessment.duration: Foundation 7 to 9 min; Higher 10 to 12 min; plus 12 min supervised preparation
assessment.content: All five themes; conversation uses two themes.
assessment.format: Role play (10 marks), picture-based task (24), conversation (36). Student chooses the first conversation topic two weeks ahead; Pearson sets the second theme. Internally conducted, externally assessed, April/May window.

assessment.title: Reading and understanding in Arabic
assessment.content: All five themes.
assessment.format: Ten questions in three sections: A in English, B in Arabic, C a translation from Arabic into English. Texts include advertisements, emails, letters, articles and literary texts.

assessment.title: Writing in Arabic
assessment.duration: Foundation 1 hour 20 min; Higher 1 hour 25 min
assessment.content: All five themes.
assessment.format: Foundation: three open-response questions and one translation into Arabic. Higher: two open-response questions and one translation into Arabic. Instructions in Arabic; vocalisation not expected.

business.subject: Business
business.label: Pearson Edexcel IGCSE 4BS1
business.statusNote: Official Pearson 4BS1 specification PDF (Issue 2, February 2026) downloaded and read as raw text (pdftotext). Paper structure, marks, weights, assessment objectives, all five content sections at numbered statement level (1.1.1 to 5.4.1), Appendix 2 command words, Appendix 3 quantitative skills and Appendix 4 formulae were compared line by line against that text. The 2027 qualification page was also opened for the 4BS1 last-assessment date. Statements are paraphrased. Year and term allocation is a recommended sequence, not a board requirement. Sample assessment materials were not opened.
business.nonExam: None: 100% external written papers. Quantitative skills are 10% of total marks across both papers, always in a business context. Six ratio formulae are provided in the exam. Assessments use International Accounting Standards terms (for example statement of financial position, inventory).

assessment.title: Investigating small businesses
assessment.content: Whole specification, set in the context of a small business (up to 49 employees, local or national market)
assessment.format: Four compulsory 20-mark questions mixing multiple choice, short answer, data response and open-ended writing; calculator allowed; June and November series; paper-based or onscreen; Level 1/2, single tier of entry; share of total marks by AO: AO1 13.7%, AO2 19.4%, AO3 11.3%, AO4 5.6%

assessment.title: Investigating large businesses
assessment.content: Whole specification, set in the context of a large business (more than 250 employees, multinational or global market)
assessment.format: Four compulsory 20-mark questions mixing multiple choice, short answer, data response and open-ended writing; calculator allowed; June and November series; paper-based or onscreen; Level 1/2, single tier of entry; share of total marks by AO: AO1 13.7%, AO2 19.4%, AO3 11.3%, AO4 5.6%

computing.subject: Computer Science
computing.label: Taught: Pearson Edexcel GCSE 1CP2 · Exam: Pearson Edexcel IGCSE 4CP0

examEntry.label: Pearson Edexcel IGCSE 4CP0
examEntry.papers: Paper 1 (4CP0/01) Principles of Computer Science: written, 2 hours, 80 marks, 50%. Paper 2 (4CP0/02) Application of Computational Thinking: a practical exam on a computer, 3 hours, 80 marks, 50%, in Python, C# or Java, with no internet, sat within a window set by Pearson.
examEntry.privateCandidates: Paper 2 needs a centre that can give the pupil a secure computer, a separate user area and Pearson's data files during the exam window. Check this with the centre before entry: not every centre that takes private candidates runs it.
notes: 4CP0 does have an on-screen paper: Paper 2 is a 3-hour practical programming exam, an hour longer than 1CP2 Paper 2 (2 hours, 75 marks). Build stamina with full 3-hour Python practice in Year 11.
Pupils keep using Python. 4CP0 also allows C# or Java; check the 4CP0 Paper 2 arrangements for the files and documents supplied in the exam.
Paper 1 is 2 hours and 80 marks (1CP2 Paper 1 is 1 hour 30 and 75 marks) and always has at least one 6-mark essay-style question.

Both courses cover the same broad areas (problem solving, programming, data, computers, networks and the internet, the wider impact of technology), but numbering and detail differ: map each 1CP2 lesson to the 4CP0 statements before Year 11 revision.
The 1CP2 Practical Programming Statement is a UK GCSE requirement; 4CP0 assesses programming directly in Paper 2.

computing.statusNote: Verified against Pearson's own specification PDF (Issue 1, January 2020), re-read as raw pdftotext -layout text: qualification overview, assessment information, Topics 1 to 6 (every section and numbered point, re-compared line by line, no differences found) and Appendix 1 command words. Paper 1 states calculators must not be used; the specification Paper 2 section and the Paper 2 sample paper cover state nothing on calculators. The Programming Language Subset Version 4 (Summer 2023) was read in full as raw text and is summarised at topic level in this file's plsSummary field; Version 6 (Summer 2025) was read only through Pearson's change summary because the full Version 6 PDF could not be located on Pearson's pages. Pearson's January 2024 subject update announces no specification changes. Units are section level (e.g. 2.1); points carry the numbered spec references. Year and term placement is a recommended sequence.
computing.tiers: None. One untiered paper set for all students, graded 9 to 1 on the total mark.
computing.nonExam: No coursework or programming project. A senior leader at each centre must complete a Practical Programming Statement, confirming students could design, write, test and refine Python programs; submit by 31 May of the exam year. Python 3 with the Pearson Programming Language Subset (PLS) supplied in the exam; any valid construct earns marks. Level 2 and computer-related maths are assessed in both papers. Graded 9 to 1 on the total mark only; below the minimum is U. Retakers must resit both papers in the same May/June series.

assessment.title: Principles of Computer Science
assessment.content: Topics 1 to 5: Computational thinking, Data, Computers, Networks, Issues and impact
assessment.format: Written paper, no calculator. Five compulsory questions, one per topic (topic order varies by series); multiple-choice, short, medium and extended open-response, tabular and diagrammatic items.

assessment.title: Application of Computational Thinking
assessment.content: Topic 6: Problem solving with programming
assessment.format: On-screen practical exam in Python 3 using the centre's IDE, no internet access. Six compulsory questions; coding files, printed paper and PLS supplied. Synoptic assessment is in this paper only. The specification and sample paper give no calculator rule for Paper 2 (Paper 1 forbids calculators).

aos.desc: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the key concepts and principles of computer science.
Apply knowledge and understanding of computer science to solve problems and write programs.
Analyse problems computationally, then design, program, evaluate and refine solutions.

commandWords.meaning: Change, add, delete or rearrange code (Paper 1: 1 to 6 marks; Paper 2: 5 to 15 marks).
Create or manipulate an artefact or program in the required notation (Paper 1: 1 to 6 marks; Paper 2: 5 to 15 marks).
Give a numerical answer with working and units if applicable (2 to 4 marks).
Fill in a table, diagram or algorithm in any notation (2 to 6 marks).
Create an artefact such as a truth table using subject symbols and rules (2 to 4 marks).
Change information from one representation to another (2 to 6 marks).
Give the meaning of a term (1 to 2 marks).
Give a linked, developed account; no justification needed (2 to 4 marks).
Identify the issue, explore all aspects, argue through reasoning (6 marks, Paper 1 only).
Produce a labelled diagram by hand or with a ruler (2 to 6 marks).
Justify or exemplify a point with reasoning, including logical or mathematical (2 to 4 marks).
Recall information; treated as synonyms (1 mark each).
Select key information from a stimulus or options (1 mark each).

gaps: Programming Language Subset Version 6 (Summer 2025) full text was not opened; the summary uses Version 4 plus Pearson's Version 6 change summary, so check the live PLS each series.
Paper 2 calculator use is not stated in the specification or sample paper; do not assume either way.
Mark allocations per topic in Paper 1 are not given in the specification and were not recorded.
Appendix 2 (flowchart symbols) was not itemised.

units.title: Computational thinking: 1.1 Decomposition and abstraction
points: Understand how decomposition and abstraction help model real-world aspects and solve problems (1.1.1).
Understand the benefits of using subprograms (1.1.2).

units.title: Computational thinking: 1.2 Algorithms
points: Follow and write algorithms as flowcharts, pseudocode or code using sequence and selection (1.2.1).
Use count-controlled and condition-controlled repetition, and iterate over every item in a data structure (1.2.1).
Cover input, processing and output in algorithms (1.2.1).
Know why variables, constants and one- and two-dimensional strings, records and arrays are needed (1.2.2).
Use arithmetic operators, including modulus, integer division and exponentiation (1.2.3).
Use relational operators and the logical operators AND, OR and NOT (1.2.3).
Find an algorithm's output for given data, using a trace table for variable values (1.2.4).
Know syntax, logic and runtime errors; identify and correct logic errors in algorithms (1.2.5).
Understand how bubble sort, merge sort, linear search and binary search work (1.2.6).
Judge fitness for purpose and efficiency: comparisons, loop passes and memory use (1.2.7).

units.title: Computational thinking: 1.3 Truth tables
points: Apply AND, OR and NOT in truth tables with up to three inputs to solve problems (1.3.1).

units.title: Data: 2.1 Binary
points: Binary represents data and instructions; count the states available for a given number of bits (2.1.1).
Represent unsigned integers and signed integers using two's complement (2.1.2).
Convert between denary and 8-bit binary: 0 to 255, and -128 to +127 (2.1.3).
Add two positive binary patterns and apply logical and arithmetic binary shifts (2.1.4).
Explain overflow when a result exceeds the available bits (2.1.5).
Explain why hexadecimal is used and convert between hex and binary (2.1.6).

units.title: Data: 2.2 Data representation
points: Represent characters using 7-bit ASCII (2.2.1).
Describe bitmap images using pixels, resolution and colour depth (2.2.2).
Describe sound sampling using amplitude, sample rate, bit depth and sample interval (2.2.3).
Explain the limits of binary representation when the number of bits is fixed (2.2.4).

units.title: Data: 2.3 Data storage and compression
points: Know storage units: bit, nibble, byte, kibibyte, mebibyte, gibibyte, tebibyte (2.3.1).
Construct expressions to calculate file sizes and data capacity requirements (2.3.1).
Explain why compression is needed and compare lossless and lossy methods (2.3.2).

units.title: Computers: 3.1 Hardware
points: Describe the von Neumann stored program concept (3.1.1).
Explain the roles of RAM, control unit, ALU, registers, clock and the address, data and control buses in fetch-decode-execute (3.1.1).
Explain the role of secondary storage and how magnetic, optical and solid-state devices store data (3.1.2).
Know what an embedded system is and what embedded systems are used for (3.1.3).

units.title: Computers: 3.2 Software
points: Describe operating system functions: file, process, peripheral and user management (3.2.1).
Describe utility software: repair, backup, compression, defragmentation and anti-malware (3.2.2).
Explain robust software and finding vulnerabilities through audit trails and code reviews (3.2.3).

units.title: Computers: 3.3 Programming languages
points: Compare characteristics and purposes of low-level and high-level languages (3.3.1).
Explain how interpreters and compilers translate high-level code into machine code differently (3.3.2).

units.title: Networks: 4.1 Networks
points: Explain why computers are connected in networks (4.1.1).
Distinguish LAN and WAN (4.1.2).
Describe how the internet is structured, including IP addressing and routers (4.1.3).
Explain how wired and wireless connections affect speed, range, latency and bandwidth (4.1.4).
Use bit-per-second speeds (kilobit, megabit, gigabit); build expressions linking file size, rate and time (4.1.5).
Explain the role and need for protocols: Ethernet, Wi-Fi, TCP/IP, HTTP, HTTPS and FTP (4.1.6).
Know the email protocols POP3, SMTP and IMAP (4.1.6).
Describe the four-layer TCP/IP model: application, transport, internet and link (4.1.7).
Describe the characteristics of bus, star and mesh topologies (4.1.8).

units.title: Networks: 4.2 Network security
points: Explain why network security matters (4.2.1).
Know how vulnerabilities are found: penetration testing and ethical hacking (4.2.1).
Know how networks are protected: access control, physical security and firewalls (4.2.1).

units.title: Issues and impact: 5.1 Environmental
points: Discuss environmental issues from digital devices: energy consumption, manufacturing, replacement cycles and disposal (5.1.1).
Weigh environmental costs against benefits when giving a reasoned view in a Discuss question (5.1.1).

units.title: Issues and impact: 5.2 Ethical and legal
points: Discuss ethical and legal issues in collecting and using personal data: privacy, ownership, consent, misuse, data protection (5.2.1).
Discuss ethical and legal issues in AI, machine learning and robotics: accountability, safety, bias, liability (5.2.2).
Explain how intellectual property is protected: copyright, patents, trademarks and licensing (5.2.3).

units.title: Issues and impact: 5.3 Cybersecurity
points: Describe malware threats: viruses, worms, Trojans, ransomware and keyloggers (5.3.1).
Explain how unpatched software and out-of-date anti-malware are exploited, and how social engineering works (5.3.1).
Explain protections: anti-malware, encryption, acceptable use policies, backup and recovery (5.3.2).

units.title: Problem solving with programming: 6.1 Develop code
points: Use decomposition and abstraction to analyse, understand and solve problems (6.1.1).
Read, write, analyse and refine programs in a high-level language (6.1.2).
Convert flowcharts and pseudocode into programs (6.1.3).
Make code readable and maintainable: layout, indentation, comments, meaningful identifiers, white space (6.1.4).
Identify, locate and correct logic, syntax and runtime errors (6.1.5).
Judge fitness for purpose and efficiency with test data: comparisons, loop passes, memory use (6.1.6).

units.title: Problem solving with programming: 6.2 Constructs
points: Identify structural components: constants, variables, initialisation, assignment, subprograms, parameters, input and output (6.2.1).
Write programs using sequence, selection, and count- or condition-controlled repetition (6.2.2).
Iterate over every item in a data structure, with single entry and exit points (6.2.2).

units.title: Problem solving with programming: 6.3 Data types and structures
points: Use primitive types (integer, real, Boolean, char) and one- and two-dimensional string, array and record types (6.3.1).
Use variables and constants (6.3.2).
Manipulate strings: length, position, substrings and case conversion (6.3.3).

units.title: Problem solving with programming: 6.4 Input/output
points: Accept and respond to user input (6.4.1).
Read from and write to CSV text files (6.4.2).
Apply validation: length, presence, range and pattern checks (6.4.3).
Apply authentication: ID and password, and lookup (6.4.4).

units.title: Problem solving with programming: 6.5 Operators
points: Use addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, modulus, integer division and exponentiation (6.5.1).
Use equal to, not equal to, less than, greater than, and their or-equal-to forms (6.5.2).
Use logical operators AND, OR and NOT (6.5.3).

units.title: Problem solving with programming: 6.6 Subprograms
points: Use built-in or library subprograms and write user-devised procedures and functions (6.6.1).
Write functions that must return a value, with or without parameters (6.6.2).
Write procedures that return no value, with or without parameters (6.6.2).
Explain global and local variables and use each appropriately (6.6.3).

english-language.subject: English Language
english-language.label: Taught: AQA GCSE 8700 · Exam: Pearson Edexcel IGCSE 4EB1

examEntry.label: Pearson Edexcel IGCSE 4EB1
examEntry.papers: One paper (4EB1/01), 3 hours, 100 marks, 100%: Section A reading questions on two unseen extracts (40 marks); Section B one directed writing task using ideas from the texts (30); Section C one discursive, narrative or descriptive piece from a choice of three (30). Optional Spoken Language Endorsement (4EB1/E), reported separately.
examEntry.privateCandidates: Exam only, with no coursework. The Spoken Language Endorsement is optional; enter it only if the centre agrees to run it.
examEntry.choice: English Language B (4EB1) rather than A (4EA1): B has no set texts and no coursework, just one exam on two unseen texts, which matches the unseen reading and writing taught for AQA 8700. A needs texts from the Pearson anthology for its exam route. Pearson notes that private candidates usually take exam-only routes.
notes: Pupils sit one 3-hour paper, not two papers of 1 hour 45 minutes: build reading and writing stamina with full-length mocks in Year 11.
Section B directed writing is new to AQA-taught pupils: write for a given audience, form and purpose, using ideas from the source texts. Teach it alongside AQA Paper 2 Question 5 viewpoint writing.
Section A covers how writers use language and structure and the links between writers' ideas and perspectives, close to AQA Paper 2 Question 4 comparison.
Section C offers discursive, narrative and descriptive tasks, so AQA Paper 1 Question 5 creative writing transfers directly.
AQA question numbers and mark splits (Questions 1 to 5) do not apply: use 4EB1 past papers and mark schemes in Year 11.
The AQA Spoken Language endorsement matches the optional 4EB1 endorsement (a presentation of up to 10 minutes).

english-language.statusNote: Structure (papers, durations, marks, weightings, AOs, spoken language endorsement) and subject content were read from the AQA 8700 specification PDF and the AQA Prepare-to-teach exam information; Paper 2 question stems from AQA specimen material 1. The Y10/Y11 placement is the recommended sequence only: AQA allows any order and flexible two-year teaching. Per-question timings are not stated by AQA in the documents opened.
english-language.tiers: None (untiered, all students sit the same papers; graded 9 to 1)
english-language.nonExam: Spoken Language endorsement (AO7 to AO9): a teacher-assessed formal presentation with questions, reported as a separate grade (Distinction, Merit, Pass or Not Classified), 0% of the GCSE grade.

assessment.title: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing
assessment.duration: 1 hour 45 minutes (includes a notional 15 minutes of reading time)
assessment.content: Section A: one 20th or 21st century prose fiction extract (reading, 40 marks, AO1, AO2, AO4). Section B: one descriptive or narrative writing task (40 marks, AO5, AO6).
assessment.format: Section A: Q1 short form (4), Q2 (8), Q3 (8), Q4 extended (20). Section B: Q5 one extended piece from a prompt or image (24 content and organisation, 16 technical accuracy).

assessment.title: Writers' Viewpoints and Perspectives
assessment.duration: 1 hour 45 minutes (includes a notional 15 minutes of reading time)
assessment.content: Section A: two linked non-fiction or literary non-fiction sources from different periods, one from the 19th century (reading, 40 marks, AO1, AO2, AO3). Section B: one viewpoint writing task (40 marks, AO5, AO6).
assessment.format: Section A: Q1 short form (4), Q2 (8), Q3 (12), Q4 extended (16). Section B: Q5 one extended piece giving a personal viewpoint for a stated audience, purpose and form (24 content and organisation, 16 technical accuracy).

assessment.title: Presenting, responding and Standard English
assessment.duration: Teacher-set; presentation guide of no more than about ten minutes
assessment.content: Assesses AO7, AO8 and AO9 through a formal presentation and responses to questions and feedback.
assessment.format: Teacher-marked on a competency basis; reported as Distinction, Merit, Pass or Not Classified. No marks. Does not count towards the 9 to 1 grade.

aos.desc: Identify and interpret explicit and implicit information and ideas; select and synthesise evidence from different texts.
Explain how writers use language and structure to create effects and influence readers, using subject terminology.
Compare writers' ideas and perspectives, and how these are conveyed, across two or more texts.
Evaluate texts critically, supporting the view with appropriate textual references.
Communicate clearly, effectively and imaginatively; adapt tone, style and register; organise for coherence and cohesion.
Use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures for clarity, purpose and effect, with accurate spelling and punctuation.
Demonstrate presentation skills in a formal setting (Spoken Language).
Listen and respond appropriately to spoken language, including questions and feedback (Spoken Language).
Use spoken Standard English effectively in speeches and presentations (Spoken Language).

commandWords.meaning: Paper 2 Q1 stem: select the correct statements from a list of true and false ones.

commandWords.meaning: Paper 2 Q2 stem: gather relevant points from both sources and explain them in prose.

commandWords.meaning: Paper 2 Q4 stem: compare ideas and perspectives and the methods used in both sources.

gaps: Per-question timing advice is not stated in the AQA documents opened (only 15 minutes notional reading time per paper); the AQA Prepare-to-teach timing sheet was not opened.
Paper 1 mark splits (Q1 4, Q2 8, Q3 8, Q4 20, Q5 40) come from the specification; AQA mark schemes and levels descriptors were not read.
Paper 2 Q2 to Q4 focus wording is from the specimen paper and the AQA exam information note; live papers may vary the focus.
Spoken Language task options and the full Pass, Merit, Distinction criteria were summarised, not read line by line.

units.title: Paper 1 Section A: Question 1, retrieval
points: Short-form question worth 4 marks, based on a stated range of lines in the extract.
Skill: identify and interpret explicit information and ideas (AO1).
Answers may quote or paraphrase; copying out a long section earns no credit.
Reading is of one 20th or 21st century prose fiction extract, printed on the paper.

units.title: Paper 1 Section A: Question 2, language
points: 8 marks, on a short stated part of the extract.
Skill: explain how the writer uses language to create effects (AO2).
Bullet points on the paper are guidance only and carry no marks.
Subject terminology is credited, from simple to sophisticated use, but analysis of effect matters most.
The same skill is assessed again in Paper 2 Q3.

units.title: Paper 1 Section A: Question 3, structure
points: 8 marks, on the structure of the whole extract.
Skill: analyse how the writer has organised the text for effect (AO2).
Advice: write in detail about two or three well-chosen structural features.
Sentence-level analysis counts only where it helps explain the structure of the whole text.

units.title: Paper 1 Section A: Question 4, evaluation
points: Extended question worth 20 marks, the largest reading question on Paper 1.
Skill: evaluate the text critically, supported by textual references (AO4).
A statement is given and students decide how far they agree with it.
Marks reward the quality of evaluation, not which position is taken.
Responses may cover the writer's methods and the reader's response, with evidence.

units.title: Paper 1 Section B: Question 5, descriptive or narrative writing
points: 40 marks: 24 for content and organisation (AO5), 16 for technical accuracy (AO6).
One extended task: describe or narrate, from a written prompt or an image.
The statement before the task sets the audience and purpose.
Marked on tone, style and register, plus organisation for coherence and cohesion.
Marked on vocabulary range, sentence variety, spelling and punctuation.
Notional 15 minutes of reading time is built into the 1 hour 45 minutes; leave time to check.

units.title: Paper 2 Section A: Question 1, true statements
points: 4 marks: choose the four true statements from a list that mixes true and false ones.
Skill: identify explicit and implicit information (AO1) in a stated part of Source A.
If more than four are chosen, only the first four in order are marked.
Two linked sources: one non-fiction and one literary non-fiction, from different periods including the 19th century.

units.title: Paper 2 Section A: Question 2, summary
points: 8 marks: a summary of the differences or similarities between the two sources, on a stated focus.
Skill: select relevant information and synthesise it across both texts (AO1).
Write in continuous prose, drawing inferences rather than listing quotations.
Use only material that answers the specific focus given in the question.

units.title: Paper 2 Section A: Question 3, language
points: 12 marks, on one source only (in the specimen, the 19th-century letter).
Skill: explain how the writer uses language to influence the reader (AO2).
Same skill as Paper 1 Q2, applied to non-fiction and literary non-fiction.
Subject terminology supports analysis of effect but does not replace it.

units.title: Paper 2 Section A: Question 4, comparison of perspectives
points: Extended question worth 16 marks, using the whole of both sources.
Skill: compare writers' ideas and perspectives and how they are conveyed (AO3).
Comparison should go beyond basic comprehension to methods: language and structure.
Both sources need balanced, supported coverage, with linking comparative language.

units.title: Paper 2 Section B: Question 5, viewpoint writing
points: 40 marks: 24 for content and organisation (AO5), 16 for technical accuracy (AO6).
One extended piece presenting the student's own view on a statement or theme linked to Section A.
Audience, purpose and form are stated (the specimen asks for a newspaper article).
Material from Section A may be used, but as the student's own view of it.
Rewards persuasive organisation, controlled register, varied sentences and accurate spelling and punctuation.

units.title: Spoken Language endorsement (AO7 to AO9)
points: A formal presentation of no more than about ten minutes, on a topic agreed with the teacher.
Students respond to questions and feedback from the audience (AO8).
Spoken Standard English must be used effectively and be audible and intelligible (AO9).
Graded Pass, Merit or Distinction on a competency basis; all criteria for a grade must be met.
Reported separately on the certificate; carries no marks and no weighting in the GCSE grade.

units.title: Subject content: reading across the course
points: Read fluently and critically a wide range of 19th, 20th and 21st century texts.
Texts include literature, literary non-fiction, reviews and journalism.
Evaluate and compare texts, and summarise and synthesise ideas across them.
Use reading to inform the student's own writing.

units.title: Subject content: writing across the course
points: Write clearly and coherently in Standard English for different purposes and audiences.
Purposes named: describing, narrating, explaining, instructing, informing, arguing.
Use accurate grammar, punctuation and spelling, and a wide vocabulary.
Use rhetorical and creative techniques for impact.

gcse-science.label: Pearson Edexcel IGCSE 4BI1 / 4CH1 / 4PH1 / 4SD0
gcse-science.statusNote: Re-read on 22 October 2026 as raw text (pdftotext) from the four official Pearson specification PDFs: Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1, Physics 4PH1 and Science (Double Award) 4SD0. Papers, codes, durations, marks, weightings, assessment objectives, command words, practical approach, grading, forbidden combinations, the maths skills table (read from the page image) and every numbered point in all 17 units were compared with the raw text: 176 Biology, 182 Chemistry and 195 Physics points, each paraphrased in this file with its spec number. A trailing B, C or P marks a bold statement: Paper 2 only and not in the Double Award; these match the Double Award PDF's own exclusion lists exactly. Year and term placement is a recommended sequence, not set by the board. The modular 2024 specifications were not read.
gcse-science.qualification: International GCSE (9-1) Biology, Chemistry and Physics (2017 specifications, linear) and International GCSE Science (Double Award)
gcse-science.tiers: None. All papers are untiered. Papers are not graded individually. Single sciences: one grade 9 to 1 from the total of 180 marks, unscaled. Double Award: 330 marks, 17-point scale 9-9 to 1-1. Paper 1 tests core content only; Paper 2 tests all content including bold statements (references B, C, P).
gcse-science.nonExam: No coursework, no practical endorsement and no separate practical paper. Practical investigations are written into the content as italicised 'practical:' points, and experimental skills (solving problems in practical contexts, planning, variables, measurement, analysis, reliability, evaluation) are examined in the written papers (AO3). Appendix 6 of each specification lists optional extra investigations. Practical points: Biology 2.9, 2.12, 2.14B, 2.17, 2.23, 2.33B, 2.39, 2.45B, 2.50, 2.58B, 3.5, 4.2, 4.4B, 5.6; Chemistry 1.7C, 1.13, 1.36, 1.60C, 2.14, 2.21, 2.42, 2.43C, 3.8, 3.15, 3.16, 4.43C; Physics 1.5, 1.22, 2.9, 2.23P, 3.17, 3.19, 3.25P, 3.27P, 4.9, 5.4, 5.11P, 5.14P, 6.6, 7.6. Double Award keeps the points without a letter: Biology 9, Chemistry 8, Physics 9 practicals. The Double Award papers (4SD0/1B, 1C, 1P) are 110 marks and 33.3% each, 330 marks in total, all taken in the same series. Calculators are allowed but not those that retrieve text or formulae or have QWERTY keyboards. Papers are in English only. Series: November and June. Physics Appendix 7 lists formulae that are not provided in the exam.

units.title: The nature and variety of living organisms

units.title: Waves
units.paper: Physics Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Physics Paper 1
points: 3.1 Units: degree, Hz, m, m/s and s.
3.2 Difference between longitudinal and transverse waves.
3.3 Definitions of amplitude, wavefront, frequency, wavelength and period.
3.4 Waves transfer energy and information, not matter.
3.5 Wave speed = frequency x wavelength (v = fλ).
3.6 Frequency = 1 / time period.
3.7 Using wave relationships for sound and electromagnetic waves.
3.8 Doppler effect: observed frequency and wavelength change for a moving source.
3.9 All waves can be reflected and refracted.
3.10 Light is part of a continuous electromagnetic spectrum travelling at the same speed in free space.
3.11 Order of the spectrum by wavelength and frequency, including visible colours.
3.12 Uses of each electromagnetic radiation, from radio waves to gamma rays.
3.13 Harmful effects of excess exposure to microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet and gamma rays, and protection.
3.14 Light waves are transverse and can be reflected and refracted.
3.15 Law of reflection: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.
3.16 Ray diagrams for reflection and refraction.
3.17 Practical: refraction using rectangular blocks, semi-circular blocks and prisms.
3.18 Refractive index n = sin i / sin r.
3.19 Practical: refractive index of glass using a glass block.
3.20 Total internal reflection carries information in optical fibres and prisms.
3.21 Meaning of critical angle c.
3.22 Critical angle and refractive index: sin c = 1/n.
3.23 Sound waves are longitudinal and can be reflected and refracted.
3.24P Human hearing range is 20 to 20 000 Hz.
3.25P Practical: speed of sound in air.
3.26P Oscilloscope and microphone display a sound wave.
3.27P Practical: frequency of a sound wave using an oscilloscope.
3.28P Pitch relates to frequency of the source's vibration.
3.29P Loudness relates to amplitude of the source's vibration.

units.title: Energy resources and energy transfers
units.paper: Physics Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Physics Paper 1
points: 4.1 Units: kg, J, m, m/s, m/s2, N, s and W.
4.2 Energy stores (chemical to nuclear) and transfers: mechanical, electrical, heating, radiation.
4.3 Use the principle of conservation of energy.
4.4 Efficiency = useful energy output / total energy output x 100%.
4.5 Explaining energy transfers in devices, including Sankey diagrams.
4.6 Thermal energy transfer by conduction, convection and radiation.
4.7 Role of convection in everyday phenomena.
4.8 Emission and absorption of radiation relate to surface and temperature.
4.9 Practical: thermal energy transfer by conduction, convection and radiation.
4.10 Reducing unwanted energy transfer, such as insulation.
4.11 Work done = force x distance moved in the force's direction.
4.12 Work done equals energy transferred.
4.13 Gravitational potential energy = mass x g x height.
4.14 Kinetic energy = half x mass x speed squared.
4.15 Conservation of energy links gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy and work.
4.16 Power is the rate of energy transfer or of doing work.
4.17 Power = work done / time taken.
4.18P Energy transfers in generating electricity: wind, water, geothermal, solar, fossil fuels, nuclear.
4.19P Advantages and disadvantages of large-scale renewable and non-renewable electricity production.

units.title: Solids, liquids and gases
units.paper: Physics Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Physics Paper 1
points: 5.1 Units: °C, K, J, kg, kg/m3, m, m2, m3, m/s, m/s2, N and Pa.
5.2P Unit: joules per kilogram degree Celsius (J/kg °C).
5.3 Density = mass / volume.
5.4 Practical: density from direct measurements of mass and volume.
5.5 Pressure = force / area.
5.6 Pressure at a point in a resting gas or liquid acts equally in all directions.
5.7 Pressure difference = height x density x gravitational field strength.
5.8P Heating changes stored energy, raising temperature or causing change of state.
5.9P Changes when a solid melts and when a liquid evaporates or boils.
5.10P Particle arrangement and motion in solids, liquids and gases.
5.11P Practical: temperature-time graph showing constant temperature during change of state.
5.12P Specific heat capacity: energy to change one kilogram's temperature by one degree Celsius.
5.13P Change in thermal energy = mass x specific heat capacity x temperature change.
5.14P Practical: specific heat capacity of materials including water and solids.
5.15 Gas molecules move randomly and exert force, hence pressure, on container walls.
5.16 Absolute zero of temperature is -273 °C.
5.17 Kelvin scale and converting between Kelvin and Celsius.
5.18 Higher temperature raises average speed of gas molecules.
5.19 Kelvin temperature of a gas is proportional to average molecular kinetic energy.
5.20 Qualitative pressure-volume and pressure-temperature relationships for a fixed amount of gas.
5.21 Fixed mass of gas at constant volume: p1/T1 = p2/T2.
5.22 Fixed mass of gas at constant temperature: p1V1 = p2V2.

units.title: Magnetism and electromagnetism
units.paper: Physics Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Physics Paper 1
points: 6.1 Units: A, V and W.
6.2 Magnets attract and repel magnets and attract magnetic substances.
6.3 Properties of magnetically hard and soft materials.
6.4 Meaning of magnetic field line.
6.5 Some materials become magnetised when placed in a magnetic field.
6.6 Practical: field pattern of one bar magnet and between two.
6.7 Producing a uniform field using two permanent magnets.
6.8 An electric current in a conductor produces a magnetic field.
6.9P Construction of electromagnets.
6.10P Field patterns for a straight wire, flat coil and solenoid carrying current.
6.11P Force on a moving charged particle in a magnetic field, unless parallel.
6.12 Force on a current-carrying wire in a field; d.c. motors and loudspeakers.
6.13 Left-hand rule predicts force direction on a wire perpendicular to the field.
6.14 How the force on a conductor changes with field and current.
6.15 Voltage is induced when a conductor moves through a field or the field changes.
6.16 Generating electricity by rotating a magnet in a coil, or a coil in a field.
6.17P Transformer structure; turns on input and output sides change alternating voltage.
6.18P Step-up and step-down transformers in electricity generation and transmission.
6.19P Voltage ratio equals turns ratio for a transformer.
6.20P Input power equals output power for 100% efficiency: VpIp = VsIs.

units.title: Radioactivity and particles
units.paper: Physics Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Physics Paper 1
points: 7.1 Units: becquerel (Bq), cm, hour, minute and second.
7.2 Atom structure of protons, neutrons, electrons; nuclide symbols such as carbon-14.
7.3 Atomic (proton) number, mass (nucleon) number and isotope.
7.4 Alpha, beta and gamma are ionising radiations from unstable nuclei, emitted randomly.
7.5 Nature of alpha, beta and gamma; distinguished by penetration and ionising ability.
7.6 Practical: penetrating power of radiations using sources or simulations.
7.7 Effect on atomic and mass numbers of alpha, beta, gamma and neutron emission.
7.8 Balancing nuclear equations for mass and charge.
7.9 Photographic film or a Geiger-Muller detector detects ionising radiation.
7.10 Sources of background radiation from Earth and space.
7.11 Source activity falls over time and is measured in becquerels.
7.12 Half-life definition; it differs between radioactive isotopes.
7.13 Simple half-life calculations on activity, including graphical methods.
7.14 Uses of radioactivity in industry and medicine.
7.15 Difference between contamination and irradiation.
7.16 Dangers of ionising radiation: mutations, cell and tissue damage, waste disposal risks.
7.17 Fission, fusion and radioactive decay can be energy sources.
7.18 Neutron-induced fission of uranium-235 releases energy as kinetic energy of products.
7.19 Uranium-235 fission gives two radioactive daughter nuclei and a few neutrons.
7.20 A chain reaction occurs when released neutrons strike other uranium-235 nuclei.
7.21 Roles of control rods and moderator in fission.
7.22 Role of shielding around a nuclear reactor.
7.23 Difference between nuclear fusion and fission.
7.24 Fusion joins small nuclei into larger ones, losing mass and releasing energy.
7.25 Fusion is the energy source of stars.
7.26 Fusion needs high temperature and pressure because protons repel electrostatically.

units.title: Astrophysics
units.paper: Physics Paper 1 and Paper 2; Science (Double Award) Physics Paper 1
points: 8.1 Units: kg, m, m/s, m/s2, N, s and N/kg.
8.2 Universe holds billions of galaxies; a galaxy holds billions of stars; Milky Way.
8.3 Why gravitational field strength g varies, and differs on other planets and the Moon.
8.4 Gravity causes moons, planets, artificial satellites and comets to orbit.
8.5 Differences in the orbits of comets, moons and planets.
8.6 Orbital speed = 2 x pi x radius / time period.
8.7 Stars can be classified by colour.
8.8 A star's colour relates to its surface temperature.
8.9 Evolution of Sun-like stars: nebula, main sequence, red giant, white dwarf.
8.10 Evolution of stars more massive than the Sun.
8.11P Absolute magnitude represents brightness at a standard distance.
8.12P Draw the main components of the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram.
8.13P Past evolution of the universe and arguments for the Big Bang theory.
8.14P Evidence for the Big Bang: red-shift and cosmic microwave background radiation.
8.15P A moving wave source changes observed frequency and wavelength.
8.16P Red-shift equation: change in wavelength / reference wavelength = galaxy velocity / light speed.
8.17P Red-shift in light from galaxies at different distances.
8.18P Why red-shift provides evidence that the universe is expanding.

geography.subject: Geography
geography.label: Taught: AQA GCSE 8035 · Exam: Pearson Edexcel IGCSE 4GE1

examEntry.label: Pearson Edexcel IGCSE 4GE1
examEntry.papers: Paper 1 Physical geography (4GE1/01): 1 hour 10 minutes, 70 marks, 40%; Section A two of river, coastal and hazardous environments; Section B one fieldwork question on the same three topics. Paper 2 Human geography (4GE1/02): 1 hour 45 minutes, 105 marks, 60%; Section A two of economic activity and energy, rural environments and urban environments; Section B one fieldwork question on those topics; Section C one of fragile environments and climate change, globalisation and migration, development and human welfare. Paper-based or onscreen.
examEntry.privateCandidates: Written papers only, with no coursework. Fieldwork is examined in the papers, so pupils still need two enquiries of their own.
notes: There is no Paper 3 and no pre-release issue evaluation: drop AQA Paper 3 practice.

Fieldwork is examined inside each paper (Section B). Pupils need one physical enquiry linked to rivers, coasts or hazards and one human enquiry linked to economic activity, rural or urban environments, each using quantitative and qualitative methods (4GE1 Appendix 6).

Options that reuse the AQA content: Paper 1 river and coastal environments (or hazardous environments, from AQA 3.1.1); Paper 2 urban environments and economic activity and energy (from AQA 3.2.1 and the 3.2.3 energy option); Section C fragile environments and climate change (from AQA 3.1.1 and 3.1.2) or development and human welfare (from AQA 3.2.2).
4GE1 needs four in-depth case studies: in each paper, one developed country and one developing or emerging country.
Rural environments has no AQA equivalent; teach it only if it replaces one of the options above.
Use 4GE1 command words (Appendix 3) and past papers in Year 11.

geography.statusNote: Paper structure, marks, weightings, AOs and SPaG read from the AQA specification-at-a-glance and scheme-of-assessment pages; content for 3.1 to 3.4 read from the AQA subject-content pages (summaries). The board's command-word glossary was not on the pages opened. Year and term allocation is a recommended sequence only; AQA allows flexible sequencing.
geography.tiers: None (single tier, linear, all exams at the end of the course)
geography.nonExam: No coursework. Fieldwork is compulsory: at least two enquiries in two contrasting environments, human and physical, on at least two outside-school visits; the centre submits a signed fieldwork statement (date, place, numbers, enquiry focus, spec link) and the work is examined in Paper 3.

assessment.title: Living with the physical environment
assessment.content: 3.1.1 natural hazards; 3.1.2 the living world; 3.1.3 physical landscapes in the UK; 3.4 skills
assessment.format: Multiple-choice, short answer, levels of response and extended prose. Section A (33 marks) all questions; B (25) all questions; C (30) any two of Questions 3, 4, 5. Includes 3 SPaG marks.

assessment.title: Challenges in the human environment
assessment.content: 3.2.1 urban issues; 3.2.2 changing economic world; 3.2.3 resource management; 3.4 skills
assessment.format: Multiple-choice, short answer, levels of response and extended prose. Section A (33 marks) all; B (30) all; C (25) Question 3 plus one of Questions 4, 5, 6. Includes 3 SPaG marks.

assessment.title: Geographical applications
assessment.content: 3.3.1 issue evaluation; 3.3.2 fieldwork; 3.4 skills
assessment.format: Section A issue evaluation (37 marks) and Section B fieldwork (39 marks), all questions. Pre-release booklet issued 12 weeks before the exam. Includes 6 SPaG marks.

aos.desc: Knowledge of locations, places, processes, environments and different scales
Understanding of geographical concepts and the interrelationships between places, environments and processes
Interpret, analyse and evaluate geographical information to make judgements (10% within fieldwork contexts)
Select, adapt and use skills and techniques to investigate questions and communicate findings (5% within fieldwork)

commandWords.meaning: Set out characteristics, patterns or features
Give reasons or causes, with development of the point
Give the main points briefly
Offer a reasoned idea from the information provided
Identify similarities and differences
Weigh up factors and reach a judgement of importance
Judge strengths and weaknesses and reach a conclusion
Support a decision or view with evidence
Weigh evidence for and against and give a reasoned judgement
Look closely at evidence or causes in detail
Base your answer on the data or source shown

gaps: AQA's own command-word glossary was not on the pages opened; the command words listed are those used in AQA question papers and should be checked against the glossary or past papers.
Content was read from AQA's web summaries of the subject content, not the full specification PDF; named-example wording should be checked against the PDF.

Options in this file: hot deserts and cold environments (one required), coasts, rivers and glaciers (two required), and food, water, energy (one required). School lessons so far show hot deserts and water; the other choices are not yet confirmed.

Fieldwork route for online pupils: the spec needs two outside-school enquiries in contrasting environments with primary data. Online pupils need an agreed route (for example supervised local fieldwork with a parent or tutor using a standard data-collection pack, or a residential or partner-centre day) and a signed centre statement. Remote or secondary data alone does not meet the requirement.
AQA assessment dates and the pre-release booklet date for the sitting were not checked.
Year and term placement is the recommended sequence, not an AQA requirement.

units.title: Natural hazards (3.1.1 The challenge of natural hazards)
points: Define a natural hazard and distinguish the main types of hazard.
Explain why some hazards carry greater risk to people than others.
Factors affecting risk include vulnerability, capacity to cope and the nature of the hazard.

units.title: Tectonic hazards (3.1.1)
points: Describe plate tectonic theory and the structure of the Earth that supports it.
Locate earthquakes and volcanoes globally and link them to plate margins.
Explain how constructive, destructive and conservative margins produce earthquakes and volcanic activity.
Distinguish primary from secondary effects and immediate from long-term responses.
Explain why people continue to live in tectonically active areas.
Evaluate monitoring, prediction, protection and planning as ways to reduce risk.
Case studies required: two named tectonic events, one in a high-income and one in a low-income country, compared.

units.title: Weather hazards (3.1.1)
points: Use the general atmospheric circulation model: pressure belts and surface winds.
Describe where tropical storms occur and link this to atmospheric circulation.
Explain how tropical storms form and develop, and describe their structure.
Discuss how climate change may alter their distribution, frequency and intensity.
Describe primary and secondary effects, and immediate and long-term responses.
Judge how monitoring, prediction, protection and planning reduce the effects.
Outline UK weather hazards and evidence that UK weather is becoming more extreme.
Case studies required: one named tropical storm, and one recent UK extreme weather event with impacts and management.

units.title: Climate change (3.1.1)
points: Use evidence for climate change from the start of the Quaternary to the present.
Explain natural causes: orbital changes, volcanic activity and solar output.
Explain human causes: fossil fuel use, agriculture and deforestation.
Give an overview of effects on people and the environment.
Mitigation: alternative energy, carbon capture, tree planting and international agreements.
Adaptation: changing farming systems, managing water supply and reducing sea-level risk.

units.title: Ecosystems (3.1.2 The living world)
points: Explain producers, consumers, decomposers, food chains, food webs and nutrient cycling within an ecosystem.
Show how changing one component affects the balance of the whole system.
Describe the distribution and characteristics of large-scale global ecosystems (biomes).
Case study required: a small-scale UK ecosystem, such as a pond or woodland.

units.title: Tropical rainforests (3.1.2)
points: Describe physical characteristics and how climate, water, soils, plants, animals and people interrelate.
Explain plant and animal adaptations and issues of biodiversity.
Describe changing rates of deforestation and its causes (farming, logging, roads, mining, energy, settlement).
Assess impacts: economic development, soil erosion and contribution to climate change.
Explain the value of rainforests to people and the environment.
Evaluate sustainable management: selective logging, conservation, ecotourism, hardwood agreements and debt reduction.
Case study required: a named tropical rainforest area.

units.title: Hot deserts (3.1.2) - option, hot deserts or cold environments
points: Describe physical characteristics and the interdependence of climate, water, soils, plants, animals and people.
Explain adaptations of plants and animals, and biodiversity issues.
Opportunities: mineral extraction, energy, farming and tourism.
Challenges: extreme temperatures, water supply and inaccessibility.
Causes of desertification: climate change, population growth, fuelwood removal, overgrazing, over-cultivation, soil erosion.
Strategies to reduce desertification: water and soil management, tree planting, appropriate technology.
Case study required: a named hot desert area.

units.title: Cold environments (3.1.2) - option, hot deserts or cold environments
points: Describe physical characteristics and the links between climate, permafrost, soils, plants, animals and people.
Explain adaptations and biodiversity issues.
Opportunities: mineral extraction, energy, fishing and tourism.
Challenges: extreme temperatures, inaccessibility, and providing buildings and infrastructure.
Explain the value of cold environments as wilderness and why they need protection.
Evaluate strategies balancing development and conservation: technology, governments, treaties and conservation groups.
Case study required: a named cold environment.

units.title: UK physical landscapes (3.1.3 Physical landscapes in the UK)
points: Locate the major upland and lowland areas of the UK.
Locate the major river systems of the UK.
Apply this overview as the base for the chosen landscape studies.

units.title: Coastal landscapes in the UK (3.1.3) - option, two of coasts, rivers, glaciers
points: Describe wave types and characteristics.
Explain weathering (mechanical, chemical), mass movement, erosion, longshore drift and deposition.
Explain how geology and rock type shape coastal forms.
Explain erosional landforms: headlands, bays, cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves, arches, stacks.
Explain depositional landforms: beaches, sand dunes, spits and bars.
Evaluate hard engineering, soft engineering and managed retreat, with costs and benefits.
Case studies required: a UK coastline with landforms, and a UK coastal management scheme.

units.title: River landscapes in the UK (3.1.3) - option, two of coasts, rivers, glaciers
points: Describe the long profile and changing cross profile of a river and its valley.
Explain erosion, transportation and deposition processes in rivers.
Explain landforms: interlocking spurs, waterfalls, gorges, meanders, ox-bow lakes, levees, flood plains, estuaries.
Explain flood risk factors: precipitation, geology, relief and land use.
Interpret hydrographs showing the precipitation-discharge relationship.
Evaluate hard engineering (dams, straightening, embankments, relief channels) and soft engineering (warnings, zoning, tree planting, restoration).
Case studies required: a UK river valley with landforms, and a UK flood management scheme.

units.title: Glacial landscapes in the UK (3.1.3) - option, two of coasts, rivers, glaciers
points: Describe the maximum extent of UK ice cover in the last ice age.
Explain freeze-thaw, plucking, abrasion, glacial movement and deposition.
Explain erosional landforms: corries, arêtes, pyramidal peaks, truncated spurs, troughs, ribbon lakes, hanging valleys.
Explain transport and deposition landforms: erratics, drumlins and moraines.
Describe economic activities in glaciated uplands: tourism, farming, forestry and quarrying.
Discuss land-use conflicts and tensions between development and conservation.
Case studies required: a UK glaciated upland with landforms, and one used for tourism with impacts and management.

units.title: Urban issues and challenges
points: Describe global urban change and the drivers of urbanisation: migration and natural increase.
Explain the rise of megacities and urban trends in high- and low-income countries.
Case study required: a major city in an LIC or NEE (location, growth, opportunities, challenges).
Challenges include slums, services, unemployment, pollution, congestion and waste.
Example required: urban planning that improves life for the urban poor.
Case study required: a major UK city (migration, opportunities, inequalities, sprawl and commuter settlements).
Example required: a UK urban regeneration project.
Describe sustainable urban living and traffic management strategies.

units.title: The changing economic world
points: Classify countries by development and quality of life; evaluate measures such as GNI, HDI and life expectancy.
Link the Demographic Transition Model to development.
Explain physical, economic and historical causes of uneven development, and the consequences.
Evaluate strategies to reduce the gap: investment, aid, Fairtrade, debt relief, microfinance, intermediate technology.
Example required: how tourism growth in an LIC or NEE reduces the development gap.
Case study required: one LIC or NEE (context, economy, TNCs, aid, environment, quality of life).
Explain UK economic change: de-industrialisation, globalisation, post-industrial economy and policy.
Example required: how modern industry can be more environmentally sustainable.
Discuss rural change, the north-south divide, and the UK's trade, cultural and political links.

units.title: Resource management (3.2.3 The challenge of resource management) - compulsory
points: Explain the importance of food, water and energy for wellbeing.
Describe global inequalities in resource supply and consumption.
Explain changing UK demand and provision for food, water and energy.
Food: demand for imports, seasonal and organic food, food miles, local sourcing, agribusiness.
Water: changing demand, water quality, and matching supply to surplus and deficit areas.
Energy: the changing energy mix, fossil fuel decline and growth of renewables.

units.title: Food (3.2.3) - option, one of food, water or energy
points: Describe global food surplus and deficit and calorie supply.
Explain rising consumption and the supply factors affecting food security.
Assess impacts of insecurity: famine, undernutrition, soil erosion, price rises and unrest.
Evaluate strategies: irrigation, hydroponics, new green revolution, biotechnology, appropriate technology.
Example required: a large-scale agricultural development with pros and cons.
Explain sustainable options: organic farming, permaculture, urban farming, waste reduction.
Example required: a local scheme in an LIC or NEE increasing sustainable food supply.

units.title: Water (3.2.3) - option, one of food, water or energy
points: Describe global water surplus and deficit patterns.
Explain rising consumption and supply factors: climate, geology, pollution, over-abstraction, poverty.
Assess impacts of insecurity: disease, pollution, reduced output and conflict.
Evaluate supply strategies: diversion, storage, dams and reservoirs, transfers, desalination.
Example required: a large-scale water transfer scheme with advantages and disadvantages.
Explain sustainable options: conservation, groundwater management, recycling and grey water.
Example required: a local scheme in an LIC or NEE increasing sustainable water supply.

units.title: Energy (3.2.3) - option, one of food, water or energy
points: Describe global distribution of energy consumption and supply.
Explain rising consumption and supply factors: geography, cost, technology and politics.
Assess impacts of insecurity on sensitive areas, economies, environment and conflict.
Compare renewable sources and non-renewable sources including fossil fuels and nuclear.
Example required: extraction of a fossil fuel with advantages and disadvantages.
Explain sustainable options: energy conservation, sustainable design, demand reduction, cleaner fossil fuel technology.
Example required: a local renewable energy scheme in an LIC or NEE.

units.title: Issue evaluation
points: Study a contemporary geographical issue drawn from compulsory content, shown through a pre-release booklet.
The booklet is issued 12 weeks before the exam; a clean copy is given in the exam.
Sources may include maps, graphs, statistics, photographs, satellite images and stakeholder statements.
Link physical (3.1) and human (3.2) themes across several scales.
Weigh stakeholders' views, advantages and disadvantages, and alternative options.
Make and justify a decision in an extended evaluative answer.

units.title: Fieldwork
points: Complete two geographical enquiries using primary data collected in the field.
The enquiries must be in two contrasting environments, with at least two outside-school visits.
Both physical and human geography must be covered, and at least one must show their interaction.
Know the six enquiry stages: question, data collection, presentation, analysis, conclusions, evaluation.
Choose and justify sampling methods and assess risks in the field.
Present and analyse data using suitable graphical, cartographic and statistical techniques.
Evaluate method, reliability and the limits of conclusions.
The school submits a signed fieldwork statement; students state their own enquiry titles in the exam.

units.title: Geographical skills
points: Cartographic: atlas and OS maps, grid references, distance, direction, gradient, relief, photographs, sketch maps.
Graphical: choose, draw and read bar, line, pie, histogram, scatter, pyramid, choropleth, isoline and flow-line maps.
Numerical: number, area, scale, ratio, proportion, frequency and data-sheet design.
Statistical: averages, spread, cumulative frequency, percentage change, percentiles and misleading presentation.
Use qualitative and quantitative data, including GIS and satellite imagery.
Enquiry and argument: frame questions and build evidenced conclusions.
Literacy: communicate clearly in writing for different audiences.

islamic-studies.subject: Islamic Studies
islamic-studies.label: Pearson Edexcel IGCSE 4IS1

assessment.title: Islamic Studies
assessment.content: Section A: life, teachings and achievements of the Prophet Muhammad. Section B: key beliefs, practices and features of the early Muslim community. Section C: living the Muslim life today.
assessment.format: Four questions in total: one from two in Section A, one from two in Section B, both in Section C. Each has short answers, a 6-mark explanation and a 12-mark response linked to a Qur'an or Hadith passage. Written in English. Available June.

aos.desc: Recall, select and communicate knowledge of relevant facts from the faith and history of Islam (10 marks assess recall).
Show understanding of key concepts and themes in the faith, history and teachings of Islam.
Analyse and interpret key questions and issues, and their significance for Islamic teaching and Muslim lives.

commandWords.meaning: One word or a single sentence recalling knowledge
State the main features of an idea, developing key points to show understanding
Show understanding of concepts using relevant facts to support an argument
Link clearly to the given text and use own or others' views for a balanced argument

units.title: Personal aspects of the Prophet's life
points: Ancestry and the main events of his early years, from birth to parenthood.
Early influences, including his parents, Abu Talib and Bahira.
His work and business before the revelation of the Qur'an.
His relationships with his wives and children.
Why his early life mattered for his later work as Allah's messenger.

units.title: The Revelation of the Qur'an
keyTerms: Laylat al-Qadr (لَيْلَةُ الْقَدْر), the Night of Power
points: The events of the Night of Power (Night of Decree).
Details of the conversation with Jibrail in the cave at Hira.
Why this experience mattered in the establishment of Islam.
The importance of the revelation of the Qur'an to Muslims.
How the Qur'an was compiled.

units.title: The Prophethood of Muhammad
keyTerms: Khatam an-Nabiyyin (خَاتَمُ النَّبِيِّين), Seal of the Prophets
points: The meaning of the title 'Seal of the Prophets'.
The importance of Muhammad's role as prophet in establishing Islam.
The opposition faced in Makkah by the Prophet and his followers.

units.title: Opposition and Hijrah
points: The events of the boycott and the Mi'raj.
The plot to kill the Prophet and the details of the flight to Madinah.
The welcome by the people of Madinah and the building of mosques there.
The significance of the Hijrah for the Prophet and the early community.
Support given to the Prophet by Abu Bakr, Ali ibn Abi Talib, Uthman and Umar.
The contribution of the Companions and the helpers (Ansar) to establishing Islam.

units.title: The Sunnah of the Prophet
points: The importance for Muslims of his teachings, deeds and sayings.
How the Sunnah was recorded.
The role of the Sunnah in establishing Islamic belief and practice.

units.title: Teachings and example of the Prophet on justice and equality
points: His teaching and example on social and economic justice.
His teaching and example on human rights.
His relationship with people of other religions.
His teaching on respect for mothers and for women.
What these teachings show about Muslim beliefs about society.

units.title: The Prophet as leader
points: His role in the establishment of the Shari'ah.
The consolidation and expansion of Islam after the Hijrah.
His treatment of opponents and prisoners.
His relationship with other communities and countries.

units.title: Battles fought by the Prophet
points: The battles fought after the Hijrah: Badr, Ohud, the Trench and Khyber.
The reasons the Prophet chose to fight each battle.
The importance of the battles for the establishment of Islam.

units.title: The Prophet's final acts and his achievements
keyTerms: Hajjat al-Wada' (حَجَّةُ الوَدَاع), the Farewell Pilgrimage
points: His final pilgrimage and sermon.
The main themes and importance of his example and teaching in his later years.
His significant achievements in society, religion and politics.
The events at his death in Madinah.

units.title: The nature of belief in Allah
points: The meaning and importance of belief in the oneness of Allah (Tawhid).
The attributes of Allah: omnipotence, creator, merciful and just.
The meaning and importance of teaching about shirk and nifaq (hypocrisy).
The characteristics of Allah as shown in the Qur'an.

units.title: Risalah
points: The nature and importance of prophethood for Muslims.
What the roles of prophets teach Muslims.
The lives of earlier prophets: Adam, Ibrahim, Isma'il, Musa, Dawud and Isa.

units.title: The holy books of Islam
points: The nature of the Tawrat, Zabur, Injil and the Scrolls of Abraham.
The importance of these holy books in the establishment of Islam.

units.title: al-Qadr
points: The nature and importance of predestination for Muslims.
How al-Qadr and free will relate to the Day of Judgment.
The significance of belief in al-Qadr for the early Islamic community.
The nature and significance of evil and suffering.

units.title: Akhirah
points: Teachings about life after death: the final judgment.
Paradise (Jannah) and hell (Jahannam).
Life in the grave and Barzakh.
How these teachings are expressed in the Qur'an.

units.title: Malaikah
points: The nature and importance of angels for Muslims.
The roles and importance of Jibrail, Mikail, Israfil and Izrael.

units.title: Shari'ah
points: The principal sources of Shari'ah law: the Qur'an and the Sunnah.
The importance of the Shari'ah in the early Islamic community.
Related sources of law: ijma (consensus) and qiyas (analogy).
The difference between halal and haram in Muslim acts.
The five categories: fard, mandub, mubah, makruh and haram.

units.title: Islamic etiquette, attitude and manners
points: Islamic etiquette in relations with other people.
Islamic attitudes to lying and harmful speech.
Islamic manners when eating.
Why correct etiquette matters, with support from the Qur'an and Sunnah.

units.title: The early leaders of the Muslim community
points: Leadership of Islam after the death of the Prophet.
The role and achievements of the early leaders.
The importance of the period of the early leaders for the Islamic community.

units.title: Shahadah
points: The nature and role of Shahadah for Muslims.
The importance of reciting the Shahadah.
How the Shahadah is used in practice.

units.title: Salah
points: The nature, significance and importance of Salah in Muslim life.
How Salah is performed: ablution, times, directions, movements and recitations.
Salah in the home, in the mosque and at Friday (Jummah) prayer.
Exemptions from Salah.

units.title: Sawm
points: The nature, role, significance and purpose of fasting in Ramadan.
Those who are exempt from fasting.
The importance of Laylat al-Qadr for Muslims today.

units.title: Zakah and Khums
points: The nature and purpose of Zakah.
The nature and purpose of Khums.
The importance of Zakah and Khums for Muslims.
The global importance of giving support to those in need.

units.title: Hajj
points: The nature, role, origins and significance of Hajj.
Key actions performed during Hajj.
The importance of Hajj for Muslims.
Benefits and challenges of attending Hajj.
Exemptions from performing Hajj.

units.title: Jihad
points: The origins, meaning and significance of jihad in Islam.
The distinction between the greater (inner) and lesser (outer) jihad.
The importance of the greater jihad in Muslim life.
Conditions for declaring lesser jihad, with reference to Surah 2:190-194 and 22:39.

units.title: Islamic festivals
points: The origins and activities of Eid-ul-Adha, Eid-ul-Fitr and Ashura.
The meaning and significance of the festivals for Muslims.

units.title: Marriage and the family
points: The significance of marriage in Islamic life.
Muslim teachings about marriage.
Muslim teachings about the purpose of families.
Ceremonies relating to birth and death, and their meaning.
The importance of procreation in strengthening the Ummah.

units.title: Muslim citizenship and religious and political leadership
points: Muslim beliefs about leadership and the responsibility of religious and political leaders.
The challenges faced by leaders of Islam in the modern world.
The challenges and responsibilities of citizenship for Muslims.
The Prophet and his successors as models of leadership.

mathematics.subject: Mathematics
mathematics.label: Taught: Pearson Edexcel GCSE 1MA1 · Exam: Pearson Edexcel IGCSE 4MA1

examEntry.label: Pearson Edexcel IGCSE 4MA1
examEntry.papers: Two papers, 4MA1/1H and 4MA1/2H: each 2 hours, 100 marks and 50%. A calculator is allowed in both, and a formulae sheet is supplied.
examEntry.privateCandidates: Written papers only, so any approved centre can enter a private candidate.
notes: Teach the 1MA1 Higher course, then add what 4MA1 examines and 1MA1 does not: differentiation of integer powers of x, gradients and turning points, and calculus applied to simple kinematics (4MA1 Higher 3.4).
Set language and notation (universal set, subsets, union, intersection, 'is an element of') and Venn diagrams with numbers of elements are examined more formally in 4MA1 (1.5).
Both 4MA1 papers allow a calculator and give a formulae sheet: practise full 2-hour, 100-mark calculator papers in Year 11. Keep non-calculator fluency, but drop 1MA1-only paper practice.
Some 1MA1 topics are not in the 4MA1 content list (for example box plots, iteration and exponential graphs). They can still be taught but are not examined.
Use 4MA1 past papers and mark schemes from the start of Year 11.

mathematics.statusNote: Structure (papers, marks, weightings, calculator rules, tiers, AO weightings, formulae) and the full content list (N1-N16, A1-A25, R1-R16, G1-G25, P1-P9, S1-S6) were read from the official Pearson 1MA1 specification PDF. Statements are paraphrased. The placement of units in Year 10 or Year 11 is a recommended sequence, not a board requirement. The school teaches the Higher tier; Foundation differences are recorded where the specification states them.
mathematics.tiers: Foundation (grades 1 to 5) or Higher (grades 4 to 9, with a grade 3 allowed for a narrow miss). A student enters one tier only, and all three papers must be sat at the same tier in the same series. The school teaches the Higher tier.
mathematics.nonExam: None. There is no coursework or controlled assessment. Total 240 marks across three papers. No formula sheet is issued: only four formulae (cone curved surface area, sphere surface area, sphere volume, cone volume) are given inside the relevant questions; every other formula must be recalled.
